context_notes: THE LESSON HELD AND SHARPENED. The previous handoff said prose acceptance criteria let the author grade their own work. This session proved it five more times, and every catch came from the instrument, never from the author: (1) the first OPEN-2 fix looked correct and did NOT work -- routesCase is EXISTENTIAL, and prose surfaces carry two branches per case, so flipping one left the other satisfying it; the real fix was at the shared predicate. (2) M14 had been MIS-SPECIFIED all along -- String.replace with a string hits the FIRST occurrence, which was the beck file's intro, outside every parsed surface; the suite's landed-check passes on a mutation that lands in the WRONG REGION, which is a gap in the check itself. (3)(4)(5) Rewriting prose orphaned three anchors and added an export, all caught as BAD TEST / roster failures rather than passing vacuously. SECOND: the ~100-column hard wrap bit THREE more times, including twice while I was writing anchors specifically to avoid it -- every new suite entry now uses a single-line anchor and says so. Use `sed -n` or `cat -A` to pick an anchor; the Read tool's rendering can differ from the bytes (a reviewer hit `then refactor.` vs the real `then refactors.`). THIRD: two unprimed reviewers, given no knowledge of what had been changed, found 7 new evasions AND 4 regressions in the work shipped hours earlier -- including F1, which defeated the OPEN-6 guard by INVERTING a clause instead of narrowing it (narrowing deletes tokens and was caught; negating keeps them). Unprimed review is not optional here. FOURTH, on scope: the shipped routing text is correct on all nine corpus cases at every tier -- three reviews now agree -- so all remaining work buys protection against FUTURE regression, with ONE exception: F2 concerns the description, which is what actually routes in production, so it is the only open item with a live behavioral edge.
